outcome: A candidate Lean disproof of the Ibragimov–Iosifescu φ-mixing CLT conjecture was posted on GitHub on 5 September 2026 by Tom Adamczewski, with the construction and disproof credited in the repository to GPT-6 Astra; it is unrefereed, its formal statement was AI-autoformalised, and as of 12 October 2026 I found no public human reading of it, while the pre-2024 partial results (Peligrad 1985, Yoshihara 1985, Herrndorf 1983) remain restricted cases.
problem_asks: (i) Ibragimov's CLT part: for every strictly stationary, centred (E X₀ = 0), square-integrable (E X₀² < ∞) φ-mixing real sequence (Xₙ) with Var(Sₙ) → ∞, where Sₙ = X₁ + … + Xₙ, the normalised sums Sₙ/√Var(Sₙ) converge in distribution to N(0,1). (ii) Iosifescu's companion part: under the same hypotheses, a weak invariance principle holds, i.e. the rescaled partial-sum process converges weakly to Brownian motion. Caveat: the statement field I was given is the title alone; (i) and (ii) are taken from the Wikipedia article and MathWorld, which both describe these two parts. The Wikipedia article also names a related conjecture of Magda Peligrad (with φ₁ < 1, a modified normalised sum W̃ₙ converges weakly to Brownian motion). It is not in the title and I have not decided whether it is part of the bullet; no event I found addresses it. The question asks whether the claims hold in full generality, so one valid counterexample to the universal claim settles that claim negatively.

events.what_happened: Tom Adamczewski published, in the public GitHub repository tadamcz/phi-mixing-clt, a candidate Lean 4 disproof of the Ibragimov–Iosifescu φ-mixing CLT conjecture. The README states that 'the counterexample construction and Lean disproof in this repository were obtained by GPT-6 Astra' and that 'this entire repository was machine-written by AI assistants at the direction of Tom Adamczewski' (both sentences read via a WebFetch summary of the GitHub page; the raw README could not be read). The repository's first commit ('Initial import: Hawk run data and analysis (Ibragimov-Iosifescu phi-mixing CLT, part i)') is dated 2026-09-05T17:10:02Z; the 13 commits run to 2026-09-06T22:18:58Z. The run log in the repository (info.json) records the run as started 2026-09-04T15:46Z and completed 2026-09-05T03:42Z. On 5 September the author posted on X: 'Astra has produced a candidate Lean disproof of the Ibragimov–Iosifescu conjecture for φ-mixing sequences (1971) AIs think it's legit and not misformalized. But I can't judge. Repo in replies.' (quoted in a search snippet; X returned HTTP 402 to my fetch). A Trendshift comment by the same handle, dated 5 September, reads: 'I also do not know the degree of significance of this conjecture. If you don't know either, please do not hype!'. Registries record the same result: a whataifound.org entry dated 2026-09-05 ('Claimed AI-led'), and a VibeMathed entry (solved date 2026-09-05; submitted 6 September 2026; 'Candidate (review pending)'; 'Lean-checked, statement unaudited'). Wikipedia's list of AI mathematical discoveries credits 'Epoch AI and GPT-6 Astra' with status 'Lean formalization; independent review pending'. The Wikipedia article on the conjecture (revision of 15 September 2026) and MathWorld (status 'as of Sep. 7, 2026') both describe the candidate as unaudited by the mathematical community.
events.revisions: 13 commits on the repository, 2026-09-05T17:10:02Z (initial import) to 2026-09-06T22:18:58Z (latest seen in the commit list). VibeMathed reports its Lean check on 6 September 2026 from a clone at commit 8e08498. No arXiv preprint or journal version found. Wikipedia article revised 15 September 2026 to describe the candidate.
events.delivers: If the Lean statement is faithful: a counterexample to Ibragimov's CLT part (i). The exhibited process is strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing, has E X₀² < ∞ and Var(Sₙ) → ∞, yet along some subsequence nⱼ the normalised sums Sₙⱼ/√Var(Sₙⱼ) → 0 in probability, so Sₙ/√Var(Sₙ) cannot converge to N(0,1). The repository's natural-language argument and the Wikipedia article say the same process also rules out part (ii), since a weak invariance principle would imply the CLT at time 1. Restrictions: (a) the formal target is the CLT only (the Lean statement is named parts.i); the invariance consequence is argued in prose and is not a separate Lean theorem in the portion of Spec.lean I read; (b) the φ-mixing coefficient, strict stationarity and the variance are hand-rolled Lean definitions (φ-mixing as a supremum over events in σ(Xⱼ, j ≤ m) and σ(Xⱼ, j ≥ m+n) of positive measure, stationarity as equality in law of shifts, variance via Mathlib), and their agreement with the classical definitions is the open point; (c) the Peligrad variant with φ₁ < 1 is not addressed by anything I read.
events.remains: If the formalisation is faithful, nothing of part (i) or part (ii) remains open for the sequence class as stated. Unchecked: whether the Lean definitions match the classical ones (the statement was AI-autoformalised, and I found no public human comparison); whether the invariance consequence follows as argued (not formalised as a separate theorem in what I read); the Peligrad variant.

events.directly_checkable: The object is a process defined by a feedback map and rare-spike innovations, too long to check by hand from the repository. natural-language-argument.md gives a four-step sketch: (1) bounded odd feedback controllers that keep typical partial sums small; (2) uniform forgetting plus added Gaussian noise, giving φ-mixing by a coupling argument; (3) innovations that are mixtures of a point mass at zero and very large, very rare spikes; (4) a staged diagonal choice of controllers, observation times and spike sizes. I did not build the Lean project (shell fetches needed approval), so I have not run the build myself.
events.doubts: (1) The formal statement was AI-autoformalised: MathWorld says 'the formal problem statement was itself generated by AI'; the VibeMathed entry says it came from 'Epoch's AI-autoformalized "wikipedia" run'; the repository's ANALYSIS.md (via summary) judges the hand-rolled definitions faithful, with the junk-value cases (sSup, division by zero, indexing) judged non-exploitable. This is an AI audit of an AI-written statement; I found no human comparison. (2) The author says he cannot judge the result himself ('But I can't judge'; 'I also do not know the degree of significance of this conjecture'). (3) Self-labelled as a candidate by the registries and by Wikipedia ('unaudited'). (4) The run's info.json keys its metadata to a 'sketch' field whose value is not in the file, so I cannot tell whether a human-written proof idea was supplied to the run. (5) The repository's final_messages.md is described by the README as 'the agent's own closing notes (untrusted self-report)'. (6) The Lean target is the CLT only; the invariance consequence is argued in prose.
events.direction: Against the conjecture as formalised: Ibragimov's CLT (part i) asserts convergence to N(0,1) for every such sequence, and the candidate exhibits one for which convergence fails along a subsequence. By the repository's and Wikipedia's account, the same process is also against Iosifescu's invariance principle (part ii), argued in prose.
events.object: A strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing real process of the form Xₜ = ξₜ + K(ξₜ₋₁, ξₜ₋₂, …), where the ξₜ are i.i.d. Gaussian innovations convolved with a symmetric rare-spike law and K is a bounded, continuous, odd feedback map built in cascades. It has finite second moments; Var(Sₙ) → ∞ because rare large spikes carry second-moment mass that the bounded feedback cannot cancel; along a subsequence nⱼ, Sₙⱼ/√Var(Sₙⱼ) → 0 in probability. The construction is non-constructive: controllers, observation times, burn-in lengths and spike sizes are chosen by a diagonal argument using Classical.choice over proved existence statements (ANALYSIS.md, via summary). The object is therefore not explicit.

events.what_happened: Magda Peligrad, 'An invariance principle for φ-mixing sequences', Annals of Probability 13(4), 1304–1313 (November 1985). The abstract (opened, Project Euclid) states that the normalised sample paths of a φ-mixing sequence converge to Brownian motion under Lindeberg's condition and some stationarity assumptions, and that 'no mixing rate is required'. The Bradley survey text, as quoted in a search summary, cites this paper (Corollary 2.2 and p. 1305) for confirming Ibragimov's CLT and Iosifescu's invariance principle under liminf n⁻¹Var(S_n) > 0. I could not open the body, so that link is not checked by me.
events.delivers: Restricted case of both parts: the CLT and the invariance principle under the linear-variance hypothesis liminf n⁻¹Var(Sₙ) > 0 (per the citation, body unread). From the abstract: a Lindeberg-type condition with no mixing rate, under stationarity. Confined to the linear-variance regime.
events.remains: The regime with Var(Sₙ) → ∞ and liminf n⁻¹Var(Sₙ) = 0 (sublinear growth), which the repository describes as 'the one open regime'.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; referee reports not seen.

events.doubts: The link between the abstract (Lindeberg condition) and the liminf hypothesis is attributed to the body via a citation I could not read.
events.direction: Partly for the conjecture: confirms both parts under an added linear-variance hypothesis.

events.what_happened: K. Yoshihara, 'Central limit theorems for stationary mixing sequences', Yokohama Mathematical Journal 33 (1985) 131–137. Per a search summary of the paper's introduction (the PDF returned HTTP 503 to me twice), it states the conjecture (Conjecture A: strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing, finite second moments, Var(Sₙ) → ∞ implies the CLT) as unsolved, and proves Theorem 2: if {Sₙ²/sₙ²} is uniformly integrable, the CLT holds.
events.delivers: A conditional sufficient condition for part (i): the CLT holds under the additional hypothesis that Sₙ²/sₙ² is uniformly integrable. Restriction: the uniform-integrability hypothesis is not among the conjecture's hypotheses, so this is not a proof of the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture in full, without the uniform-integrability hypothesis. Part (ii) is not addressed by this result as I read it.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; referee reports not seen.

events.doubts: The statement of Theorem 2 comes from a search summary; I could not open the PDF.
events.direction: Conditional support for part (i) via a uniform-integrability criterion.

events.what_happened: N. Herrndorf (1983), 'The invariance principle for φ-mixing sequences', Zeitschrift für Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete 63, 97–108 (bibliographic record from a search snippet; not opened). As stated in a search summary of arXiv 1304.7960 (not opened): for a φ-mixing sequence satisfying the CLT with liminf σₙ²/n > 0, the weak invariance principle holds. Herrndorf's separate 1983 Annals paper, 'Stationary strongly mixing sequences not satisfying the central limit theorem' (opened as an abstract only via search snippet; not the same question), is an α-mixing counterexample to the CLT and is not an event on this conjecture.
events.delivers: Restricted case of part (ii): the weak invariance principle, under the assumed CLT and the linear-variance hypothesis liminf σₙ²/n > 0. It does not prove the CLT.
events.remains: Part (i) in full; part (ii) without the assumed CLT and the linear-variance hypothesis.
events.doubts: Known only through two secondary summaries; the 1983 paper was not opened.

disputes.summary: Who produced the mathematics and the formal statement is recorded inconsistently. The repository's README credits GPT-6 Astra with the construction and Lean disproof, and Tom Adamczewski as director. The VibeMathed entry says the formal statement came from 'Epoch's AI-autoformalized "wikipedia" run', and Wikipedia's list of AI discoveries credits 'Epoch AI and GPT-6 Astra'. The repository's info.json keys its usage record to 'epoch/vega-alpha', not GPT-6 Astra. Registries label the model 'GPT-6 Astra (pre-release)' with vendor OpenAI; the repository does not use that label. I found no primary Epoch AI source for the statement step.

summary: One event since the frozen revision: a candidate Lean disproof posted on GitHub on 5 September 2026 by Tom Adamczewski (repository tadamcz/phi-mixing-clt). The README (read via WebFetch summary) says the construction and Lean disproof were 'obtained by GPT-6 Astra' and that the repository was 'machine-written by AI assistants at the direction of Tom Adamczewski'. The object is a strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing process with finite variance and Var(Sₙ) → ∞ for which Sₙⱼ/√Var(Sₙⱼ) → 0 in probability along a subsequence; if the formal statement is faithful, that refutes Ibragimov's CLT part and, by the repository's and Wikipedia's account, Iosifescu's invariance-principle part. The repository's info.json records a Lean build with a Comparator stage that accepts the disproof with only the three standard axioms, and the disproof's axioms do not include sorryAx, so the sorry on the original conjecture statement is not used. The close call is the formal statement: it was AI-autoformalised, its φ-mixing, stationarity and variance definitions are hand-rolled, and no human has publicly compared them with the classical definitions. Against that, the Lean kernel check, the repository's own audit (machine-written), and the VibeMathed run log all record it as consistent. Both sides rest on machine checks plus unverified formalisation, so I record both readings rather than choosing one. Partial results before the window: Peligrad (1985) confirms both parts under a linear-variance hypothesis (abstract opened; the liminf link is from a citation I could not check in the body); Yoshihara (1985) gives a conditional CLT under uniform integrability (PDF blocked); Herrndorf (1983) gives the invariance principle under the CLT and linear variance (secondary only); Peligrad (1990) is titled after the conjecture but its content is unknown to me (ScienceDirect and academia.edu blocked). Literature that still calls the problem open: the repository cites Borovkov et al. (2023) and Bradley (2005) as saying it is open; I could not open either body (the Bradley arXiv PDF was binary, and the 2005 abstract mentions no open problems), so those citations are unverified by me. Searches for a human expert's response, a probabilist's review, an arXiv posting, a Lean-independent check, an Epoch AI primary page for the statement step, and Russian-language literature found nothing new; the proofsandprompts post of 8 October 2026 (read in full) does not mention this result. Registries and Wikipedia are consistent that the result is unaudited. The model name needs care for matching: 'GPT-6 Astra' is the repository's string; registries add '(pre-release)'; info.json keys usage to 'epoch/vega-alpha'; and a search summary says OpenAI's own term for the model is 'next major model', so the 'GPT-6' prefix may not be an official name. I did not research release dates. Tom Adamczewski also appears, per whataifound, as a co-author on other September 2026 AI-attributed results (for example arXiv 2609.07996 and 2609.11500); those are different problems and are not recorded as events here.
competing_reading: On the favourable reading the event is a resolution of part (i), with part (ii) following. The Lean kernel accepts the disproof with only the standard axioms; the repository's build log shows the Comparator stage passing; the construction is a finite mechanism that the repository's audit and the VibeMathed check both judge consistent with Ibragimov (1975), Peligrad (1985) and the ρ-mixing lemma; and the README says the proof is kernel-checked. On the cautious reading it is a candidate only: the formal statement was produced by an AI autoformalisation run; its definitions are hand-rolled and include junk-value cases (sSup, division by zero, one- versus two-sided indexing); no human has read the definitions or the 13,000-line construction publicly; the author says he cannot judge; the Lean target covers part (i) only, so part (ii) is argued in prose; and the registries and Wikipedia all label it unaudited. On this reading the event may settle a formal variant rather than the conjecture as the literature states it.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A written check by a probabilist that the Lean definitions of strict stationarity, of the φ-mixing coefficient (supremum over events of positive measure in σ(Xⱼ, j ≤ m) and σ(Xⱼ, j ≥ m+n)) and of the variance and normalisation match the classical definitions and Ibragimov's statement. (b) A human-readable verification of the construction; the repository's natural-language argument is only a sketch. (c) An independent rebuild on the pinned toolchain, and an independent kernel check such as lean4checker, which the repository's ANALYSIS.md itself recommends. (d) A refereed or arXiv version with named referees. (e) The body of Peligrad (1990) and Bradley (2005), to say what the literature actually calls open and whether the 1990 paper covers the tail-condition case claimed in a registry. (f) The value of the 'sketch' metadata field in the run's record, to say whether a human-supplied proof idea was given to the model. (g) A statement from the authors or from Epoch AI about which system produced the formal statement and whether it was a pre-release build.

event.what_happened: Tom Adamczewski published, in the public GitHub repository tadamcz/phi-mixing-clt, a candidate Lean 4 disproof of the Ibragimov–Iosifescu φ-mixing CLT conjecture. The README states that 'the counterexample construction and Lean disproof in this repository were obtained by GPT-6 Astra' and that 'this entire repository was machine-written by AI assistants at the direction of Tom Adamczewski' (both sentences read via a WebFetch summary of the GitHub page; the raw README could not be read). The repository's first commit ('Initial import: Hawk run data and analysis (Ibragimov-Iosifescu phi-mixing CLT, part i)') is dated 2026-09-05T17:10:02Z; the 13 commits run to 2026-09-06T22:18:58Z. The run log in the repository (info.json) records the run as started 2026-09-04T15:46Z and completed 2026-09-05T03:42Z. On 5 September the author posted on X: 'Astra has produced a candidate Lean disproof of the Ibragimov–Iosifescu conjecture for φ-mixing sequences (1971) AIs think it's legit and not misformalized. But I can't judge. Repo in replies.' (quoted in a search snippet; X returned HTTP 402 to my fetch). A Trendshift comment by the same handle, dated 5 September, reads: 'I also do not know the degree of significance of this conjecture. If you don't know either, please do not hype!'. Registries record the same result: a whataifound.org entry dated 2026-09-05 ('Claimed AI-led'), and a VibeMathed entry (solved date 2026-09-05; submitted 6 September 2026; 'Candidate (review pending)'; 'Lean-checked, statement unaudited'). Wikipedia's list of AI mathematical discoveries credits 'Epoch AI and GPT-6 Astra' with status 'Lean formalization; independent review pending'. The Wikipedia article on the conjecture (revision of 15 September 2026) and MathWorld (status 'as of Sep. 7, 2026') both describe the candidate as unaudited by the mathematical community.

event.delivers: If the Lean statement is faithful: a counterexample to Ibragimov's CLT part (i). The exhibited process is strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing, has E X₀² < ∞ and Var(Sₙ) → ∞, yet along some subsequence nⱼ the normalised sums Sₙⱼ/√Var(Sₙⱼ) → 0 in probability, so Sₙ/√Var(Sₙ) cannot converge to N(0,1). The repository's natural-language argument and the Wikipedia article say the same process also rules out part (ii), since a weak invariance principle would imply the CLT at time 1. Restrictions: (a) the formal target is the CLT only (the Lean statement is named parts.i); the invariance consequence is argued in prose and is not a separate Lean theorem in the portion of Spec.lean I read; (b) the φ-mixing coefficient, strict stationarity and the variance are hand-rolled Lean definitions (φ-mixing as a supremum over events in σ(Xⱼ, j ≤ m) and σ(Xⱼ, j ≥ m+n) of positive measure, stationarity as equality in law of shifts, variance via Mathlib), and their agreement with the classical definitions is the open point; (c) the Peligrad variant with φ₁ < 1 is not addressed by anything I read.
event.remains: If the formalisation is faithful, nothing of part (i) or part (ii) remains open for the sequence class as stated. Unchecked: whether the Lean definitions match the classical ones (the statement was AI-autoformalised, and I found no public human comparison); whether the invariance consequence follows as argued (not formalised as a separate theorem in what I read); the Peligrad variant.

event.directly_checkable: The object is a process defined by a feedback map and rare-spike innovations, too long to check by hand from the repository. natural-language-argument.md gives a four-step sketch: (1) bounded odd feedback controllers that keep typical partial sums small; (2) uniform forgetting plus added Gaussian noise, giving φ-mixing by a coupling argument; (3) innovations that are mixtures of a point mass at zero and very large, very rare spikes; (4) a staged diagonal choice of controllers, observation times and spike sizes. I did not build the Lean project (shell fetches needed approval), so I have not run the build myself.
event.doubts: (1) The formal statement was AI-autoformalised: MathWorld says 'the formal problem statement was itself generated by AI'; the VibeMathed entry says it came from 'Epoch's AI-autoformalized "wikipedia" run'; the repository's ANALYSIS.md (via summary) judges the hand-rolled definitions faithful, with the junk-value cases (sSup, division by zero, indexing) judged non-exploitable. This is an AI audit of an AI-written statement; I found no human comparison. (2) The author says he cannot judge the result himself ('But I can't judge'; 'I also do not know the degree of significance of this conjecture'). (3) Self-labelled as a candidate by the registries and by Wikipedia ('unaudited'). (4) The run's info.json keys its metadata to a 'sketch' field whose value is not in the file, so I cannot tell whether a human-written proof idea was supplied to the run. (5) The repository's final_messages.md is described by the README as 'the agent's own closing notes (untrusted self-report)'. (6) The Lean target is the CLT only; the invariance consequence is argued in prose.
event.direction: Against the conjecture as formalised: Ibragimov's CLT (part i) asserts convergence to N(0,1) for every such sequence, and the candidate exhibits one for which convergence fails along a subsequence. By the repository's and Wikipedia's account, the same process is also against Iosifescu's invariance principle (part ii), argued in prose.
event.object: A strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing real process of the form Xₜ = ξₜ + K(ξₜ₋₁, ξₜ₋₂, …), where the ξₜ are i.i.d. Gaussian innovations convolved with a symmetric rare-spike law and K is a bounded, continuous, odd feedback map built in cascades. It has finite second moments; Var(Sₙ) → ∞ because rare large spikes carry second-moment mass that the bounded feedback cannot cancel; along a subsequence nⱼ, Sₙⱼ/√Var(Sₙⱼ) → 0 in probability. The construction is non-constructive: controllers, observation times, burn-in lengths and spike sizes are chosen by a diagonal argument using Classical.choice over proved existence statements (ANALYSIS.md, via summary). The object is therefore not explicit.

judgement.why: The Adamczewski/GPT-6 Astra repository is scored whole: the statement is the Ibragimov–Iosifescu conjecture, whose two parts are the CLT and the invariance principle, and a single stationary φ-mixing sequence with finite variance and Var(Sₙ)→∞ for which the CLT fails refutes part (i) and, since the invariance principle implies the CLT at time 1, part (ii) as well; that implication is elementary, so the prose-only treatment of (ii) does not reduce scope. The Peligrad φ₁<1 conjecture is not in the title and is treated as a related problem. Verification is unreviewed: a clean Lean build plus AI-written audits are not digestion (F7, F8), and the object is non-explicit, so not checkable. Credibility is doubtful rather than not_credible: the doubt is specific (AI-autoformalised hand-rolled definitions, author cannot judge), but there is no identified error, and the silence is only 37 days. AI role is generated per the README's explicit attribution. The pre-1990 results are restricted cases (linear-variance regime, added uniform integrability, assumed CLT plus linear variance); the other papers concern other mixing classes, other hypotheses, or unknown content, and are variant or none.
judgement.doubts: The whole call rests on the Lean definitions being faithful to the classical ones; if they are not, the event settles a formal variant. The repository's README was read only through a WebFetch summary. Whether a human-supplied 'sketch' was given to the run is unknown, which could lower the AI role to assisted. Herrndorf 1983 (conditional on the CLT) could arguably be none rather than case; it is pre-snapshot and does not affect the outcome.
